channel.title: The Beholder's Gazette

item.title: Bard's Suggestion Spell Makes 900 Voters Agree With a Goat
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: A bard cast Suggestion to warm up a Brindlemoor rally. Then 900 voters agreed with both candidates, a heckler and a goat. The Board would like a word.
item.content:encoded:
A bard hired to warm up the crowd at a Burgess rally in Brindlemoor cast the Suggestion spell on Tuesday night, and 900 voters spent the next eight hours agreeing with everything they heard. That included both candidates, a heckler, and a goat. The Brindlemoor Board of Elections opened an inquiry Wednesday morning.

The bard, Jessamy Pipwell of the Warm Welcome Company, was paid 6 silver by the campaign of Ada Plumtree, who is standing for the Tanner's Row seat. Her instructions, according to a contract I have read and the Board has now read twice, were "get them in a good mood." Pipwell took the stage at the Corn Exchange at seven, played two verses of a drinking song, and said "agree with everything you hear tonight" with a flourish of her lute.

I will note for the record, as the Board did, that the Suggestion spell is written for one creature. Pipwell says she aimed it at "the crowd, generally." Her party's wizard, a gnome who gave his name as Fosk and nothing else, said the acoustics in the Corn Exchange are "very good, unfortunately."

The lady from Tanner's Row spoke first. Plumtree promised to fix the gutters on Tanner's Row, and 900 people agreed. Her opponent, the gentleman from the Dyers' Guild, Hesketh Wardle, then said the gutters were fine and Plumtree was lying about them. All 900 agreed with that too. By my tally the evening produced Promises Made: 31, Promises Agreed With: 27,900, Promises Kept: none. The gutters are as they were.

At about half past eight a tanner at the back shouted, "You're both frauds and this hall smells of glue." The crowd agreed with him warmly and went on agreeing with the candidates. Then a goat named Pudding, brought by a dairywoman who could not find a sitter, said "baa." The hall agreed with the goat. Several voters have since told the Board they still agree with the goat, though none can say about what.

Clerk of Polls Ivo Thatchley, who chairs the Board, said the inquiry will decide whether a rally held under an enchantment counts as campaigning, entertainment, or one assault on 900 people. "Campaign spending rules allow bunting, ale, and one band," he said. "A bard is a band. That is the problem." A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me Wardle's campaign wants the whole rally struck from the record, while Plumtree's wants credit for the agreeing.

This is the Council's second try at an orderly by-election this month, the first having ended when a mimic ate 31 ballots. It is also the second bard in a month to talk her way into civic life; the last one became Tollwick's gate guard. Pipwell, reached at the Sleeping Mule, said she regrets nothing and now charges 9 silver.

Pudding is not on the ballot. Pudding is polling at forty percent.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Salamander Oven Subscription Lapses Mid-Bake; 40 Pies Half-Done
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: The Grand Feast's salamander oven stopped heating at noon when its heat subscription lapsed. Forty test pies came out half-baked. Still a great oven.
item.content:encoded:
Okay. OKAY. The Grand Feast committee ran its first test bake this morning, and at noon sharp the salamander oven's heat subscription failed to renew, mid-bake, with 40 pies inside. Every pie came out golden on top and raw on the bottom. Quick backstory for anyone new: Feastwarden Odo Plumbrook promised to feed 2,000 guests on the Town Green on the 26th, on a budget of 900 gp, and rented this oven from Cinderlatch Works with the heat billed separately.

I was there with my slate. For the first hour it was glorious. The committee had sprung for the Blaze tier at 12 gp a day, the salamander was coiled on its firebrick glowing a healthy orange, and the mana throughput was so high the mica window fogged. Forty pies went in: apple, mutton, and one turnip, because the treaty requires a turnip.

At noon the Blaze tier tried to renew itself out of the feast purse. The purse had 11 gp in it. A little brass bell on the oven went ding, a glowing firmware glyph came up on the door reading YOUR HEAT HAS PAUSED, and the salamander dropped to Ember, the free tier, right there in front of us. It uncoiled, turned to face the back wall, and went from a roar to the warmth of a sleeping cat.

The runic latency on that downgrade? Instant. Honestly impressive. The renewal button, meanwhile, needed a wax seal, a witness, and a twenty-minute wait for a courier from Cinderlatch.

By then the pie tops were done and the bottoms were batter. Marigold Tunney, a volunteer baker who had been up since four rolling crust, cut one open. "That's a lid," she said. "Somebody baked me forty lids."

Dobb Wrenfield, Cinderlatch's spokesman, arrived with the courier and a pamphlet. "The oven never stopped," he told me. "It stepped down to a gentler experience. Ember is our most popular tier." I asked whether anyone pays for Ember. He said that is why it's popular.

Plumbrook climbed onto a flour barrel and did the math out loud. "Forty half pies," he said, "is twenty whole pies. We are ahead of where we were yesterday." Nobody had the heart to point out that yesterday there was also no raw dough on the floor.

Fire Marshal Tamsin Coalhurst inspected the salamander and ruled it "cold enough." Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor asked how the renewal got paid. Plumbrook had found the missing gold piece in his other coat, which leaves the feast purse at 0 gp and a coupon. "We are aware of the pies," the Reeve said.

My familiar Byte, a pseudodragon who now speaks only in ad copy, hopped onto the oven and announced, "Don't let your pie go half-baked. Upgrade today." Then he ate the turnip one. Brother Tumbleberry has already sent the committee a note saying his grandmother baked pies in a hole in the ground. I've seen the Town Green. It already has holes. Duchess dug them.

Rating: four out of five beholder eyes. The salamander oven is the finest piece of kitchen hardware I've ever touched, for exactly as long as you can pay it.

Damage Report: Pies baked: 20, technically, in 40 halves. Feast purse: 0 gp and a coupon. Days to Feast Day: 7. Eyebrows: fine. Byte: full.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

item.title: Piercers Fall in Mine; Guild Sends Party Hats, Not Helmets
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: Piercers kept dropping on an adventuring party mining the Coldseam for a share of the ore. They asked the guild for helmets. The guild sent hats.
item.content:encoded:
The piercers fell, the adventuring party asked for helmets, and the guild sent hats.

An adventuring party between jobs signed on to work the Coldseam silver mine this winter "for a share of the ore." On their third shift, piercers started dropping from the ceiling of the east gallery. The party wrote to the Honorable Company of Ore-Getters, which runs the mine, and asked for four iron helmets. On Tuesday a crate arrived. Inside were four knitted wool hats with pompoms.

"I opened the crate and thought, that's a lot of padding for four helmets," said Marta Thrask, the party's fighter and, for the season, its lead pick. "Then I kept digging. It was all padding."

For anyone who hasn't worked a deep seam: a piercer looks like a stalactite until it lets go. It drops point first on whatever walks under it. The east gallery has a lot of stalactites. Nobody can say how many of them are rock.

The crate came with a scroll from Provost Ambrel Quillstone, the Company's head of shaft welfare. It said the Company "has responded to concerns with a seasonally appropriate headwear solution" and "remains committed to a warm and positive work environment." Let me translate. That means they sent hats. A warm work environment means your ears are warm while something heavy lands on them.

The hats are the Company's own colors, blue and gold. Each one has the Ore-Getters' crest stitched on the front, which Thrask points out makes a nice target.

"The pompom took the first hit," said Orlo Fennimere, the party's cleric. "The pompom did not survive. I've cast cure wounds eleven times since Monday and I came here to mine." He has started charging the rest of the party a copper a spell. I've told him to put that in writing and keep a copy.

About that share of the ore. The contract promises the party one share for every forty the Company takes. After four shifts that comes to a lump of silver the size of a dried pea. Pip Loamsby, the party's rogue, has been carrying it in her cheek "so nobody can audit it."

Provost Quillstone came down Wednesday to inspect. He wore a hat. Then he looked up, saw the gallery ceiling, and went back up the shaft in what Thrask timed at under a minute. He sent a second note that afternoon recommending "mindful walking."

Over in the money pages, Sterling Vanmoor wrote that the Ore-Getters' hats are "a lean answer to a cost question." I've worked under a lot of ceilings, Sterling. Not one of them cared what I had on my head.

The party has stopped work in the east gallery until four helmets arrive. They also want hazard pay. And they want the pea weighed in front of witnesses. Ludo Sarne, the party's wizard, keeps a mage hand floating overhead in the meantime. It holds an umbrella.

Every miner I ever worked with knew this by their second week: if the ceiling can kill you, you get a helmet. Thrask says she'll keep the hat, though. "It's warm," she said. "I'll wear it to the bar when I'm paid. If I'm paid."

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Major Image Gold Vanishes in Audit; Party Had Borrowed on It
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: An adventuring party banked 6,400 gp of dungeon loot. The audit found 2,000 gp was Major Image gold, and they had already borrowed against it.
item.content:encoded:
An adventuring party's 6,400 gp deposit at Ledgerhall Counting House shrank to 4,400 gp on Tuesday, when the year-end audit found that 2,000 gp of it was Major Image gold. The Hollowcrown Company had carried the coins out of a treasure room on the Undermaw's sixth level in September, and in October they borrowed 1,500 gp against the full balance.

On the Loaf Index, at roughly 5 copper a loaf, the missing gold is 40,000 loaves. The loan is another 30,000. (I have checked this four times. The second time I had to sit on the floor.)

Ledgerhall holds its audit each November, because the skeleton clerks on the third floor do not keep a calendar and nobody has asked them to. A clerk walks the vault and casts dispel magic on every shelf. Most years this finds a mimic. This year, one sack on shelf 31 made a small sound like a candle being blown out, and the shelf was empty.

A Major Image cast at high enough power lasts until someone dispels it. Whoever stocks that treasure room knows this. The coins looked right, clinked right, and smelled faintly of dungeon. They also weighed nothing, which is where I get cross. Two thousand gold pieces weigh forty pounds. I looked it up. The party's porter, a Fish Street lad named Tobin, says he carried the heavy sack the whole way up. Their fighter, Ottilie Marsh, carried the other one and told me she assumed she was simply very strong.

"We did think about weighing it," said the party's wizard, Fenna Drollwick. "Then we thought about lunch."

The loan is the hard part. Ledgerhall lent 1,500 gp against a balance that has now lost a third of itself, and the Hollowcrown Company spent the money on a cart, a mule, and a deposit on rooms over a cooper's. The counting house wants 2,000 gp of fresh collateral by the end of the month or it will call the loan. The party has the mule. Malgrim Dusk-Vael, Chief Executive Lich of Vaultmere Holdings, which bought Ledgerhall in the skeleton-clerk merger, said in a statement that "gold which cannot survive an audit was never on the books in any meaningful sense." Dusk-Vael added that the shelf has been relet.

This is the economics of it, and I am sorry. A lender values your collateral at what it is worth on the day it checks, and the day it checks is usually the worst day for you. Last week Sterling Vanmoor called dungeon gold "the safest asset under the realm." Sterling has never been on the sixth level.

My aunt Marigold keeps her savings in a boot. She shook it at me this morning so I could hear it clink, and then she made me hold it. It was heavy. I have never been so relieved by a boot.

What this means for your pantry: before you borrow against dungeon gold, put it on a scale. You can hire one for about a loaf a week.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Harpy Jingle Walks Party Into River; Shop Calls It Foot Traffic
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: A harpy-sung winter sale ad led an adventuring party into the Tumblebrook on Tuesday. The shop owner calls it foot traffic. I call it a funnel.
item.content:encoded:
A harpy jingle written for a winter sale marched an adventuring party called the Ninefold Spoons straight into the Tumblebrook on Tuesday morning, all five of them humming. The ad was sung by Shrillwing & Daughters, a harpy jingle troupe hired by Fernsley's Outfitters, which sits on the far bank of the river. The bridge is two hundred feet downstream. The song does not mention the bridge.

Some people see a near-drowning. I see the most frictionless customer journey Brindlemoor has ever produced. The Spoons heard the tune from the shop roof, locked eyes on the sign, and walked in a dead straight line, which is exactly what every merchant wants from a customer. The river was simply not in the plan.

The jingle, for the record, goes: "Fernsley's, Fernsley's, down by the water, cloaks are half off and the boots are a quarter." I have hummed it eleven times while writing this. My editor has asked me to close the window.

"Great foot traffic," said Hobb Fernsley, the owner, while wringing out a wizard's hat on his porch. "Wet foot traffic, sure. But they arrived, they browsed, and they converted." They did convert. The winter sale, it turns out, has a small line of print excluding "customers who are currently dripping," so the Spoons bought five dry cloaks at full price. That's 40 gp of pure upside from one verse. Hobb is a visionary and I would like to be in his mastermind circle.

The party's cleric, Wenna Thorp, had wool stuffed in her ears before the walk. "I was fine," she told me from a bench, still wet to the shins. "But I was roped to the fighter, and he was really feeling the chorus." The rogue reached the far bank first and tried to haggle on arrival. Brindlemoor's river wardens, the original disruption-haters, now want a permit for any harpy singing within a bowshot of water. Classic regulators. They never ask what the river wants.

Mistress Corva Shrillwing, who leads the troupe with her three daughters, told me the harpy jingle performed "well above projections." She has already pitched a spring version for a fishmonger on Quillmarch Bridge. I asked whether it would lead customers off the bridge. She smiled with a great many teeth and said they were "still workshopping the hook." In my world we call that iteration.

I once shared a sauna with a guildmaster at a Waterdeep trade fair, and he told me, "Sterling, attention is the only currency that doesn't sink." He was wrong about the sinking part, as the Spoons can now confirm, but right in spirit. Meanwhile my colleague Brakka Stonesweat is reportedly drafting a column about "consent." Brakka, buddy, nobody asked the river either.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

• Meet the customer where they are, even mid-river.
• A good jingle closes faster than a good bridge.
• Always read the fine print, unless you are the one who wrote it.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Thunderwave Ends Tavern Brawl; Tavern Gains a Room
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A wizard ended a tavern brawl at the Sleeping Mule with Thunderwave and blew out a wall. His party got the bill. The keeper got a room. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after midnight, a wizard allegedly ended a tavern brawl at the Sleeping Mule on Tanner's Row by casting Thunderwave in the middle of the common room. The brawl stopped at once. So did the east wall, which is now in the alley, and Keeper Bess Harrowgate has billed the wizard's adventuring party, the Rattlepan Company, 63 gold and 4 silver for it.

The fight allegedly started over a game of knucklebones and a disputed pie. By the time I got there, which was fast, because I heard it from two streets over and also felt it in my teeth, there were eleven people on the floor, one on the bar, and a very confused goat in the alley who had not been involved at all.

"He said 'everybody stop,' and then he made everybody stop," said Wim Tallis, a cooper who was holding a tankard at the time and is still holding it, because he cannot open his hand. "I flew about fifteen feet. The tankard came with me. Good tankard."

The wizard, a gnome named Alder Quist, told the City Watch the spell was "a measured response." A Watch sergeant measured the hole. It is fourteen feet across. Quist allegedly said he had aimed it at the floor, then at the ceiling, and then admitted he had not aimed it.

The Rattlepan Company's fighter, Brega Holm, said the party only came in for supper. "We didn't start it. We did finish it. We finished the wall too, I suppose." Their rogue allegedly tried to argue the wall was already loose. Harrowgate allegedly showed him the receipt for the wall.

Also, one of the brass hinges from the old east shutter landed right by my foot and it is a very nice hinge. It has a little lion on it. I am allegedly holding it for evidence. Anyway.

Harrowgate is not upset, which I found upsetting. By breakfast she had hung a curtain across the gap, put a cot in the rubble, and painted a sign that says THE THUNDER ROOM, 5 SILVER A NIGHT, BREEZE INCLUDED. A traveling bard has allegedly booked it through spring because, he says, the acoustics are now "open." Duchess, the giant boar who rents the big stall out back, has been in twice to look at it. Harrowgate says Duchess cannot afford it.

"House rule four is no spells indoors," Harrowgate told me. "House rule nine is you break it, you bought it. They bought a wall. I'm renting the wall's absence. That's just business." She has also added a house rule twelve, which reads "Thunderwave counts," because the wizard allegedly argued it was a sound and not a spell.

The Rattlepan Company has two weeks to pay. Quist allegedly offered to cast Mending on the wall. Harrowgate told him Mending fixes a cup, not a wall, and to go stand somewhere quieter. Innkeepers have wanted damage deposits from adventuring parties ever since that Fish Street inn burned, and this morning three more signed on. Hollis Delvewright will allegedly write it up as a ledger. I was there for the bang.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Levitation Slippers Recalled; Rogue Stuck on Vault Ceiling
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Driftsole recalled its 55 gp levitation slippers after 400 wearers got stuck on ceilings. One rogue found out mid-heist, in the vault. Four eyes.
item.content:encoded:
Driftsole Works has recalled its Featherstep levitation slippers, 55 gp a pair, after 400 wearers around Brindlemoor got stuck to their own ceilings. I can personally confirm one of them. Dabney Fenwhistle, rogue of the Seventh Spoon Company, bought a pair on Tuesday for a quiet heist at the Ledgerstone Vault and spent the whole job pressed flat against the vault ceiling, in full view of the guards. I was there as the party's gear consultant. I brought snacks.

Okay. First: these slippers are GORGEOUS. Soft gray felt, a little silver rune on each toe, and a firmware glyph that lets you rise, hover, and come back down with a click of the heels. The mana throughput is unreal. Dabney floated over the pressure plates like a dandelion seed and I actually gasped out loud, which a heist does not want. My pseudodragon Byte, who now speaks only in ad copy, whispered, "Rise above the competition."

Then Dabney clicked his heels to come down. The slippers read the click as "up, but more." Driftsole's notice lists the runic latency on the descend command as "unbounded," which I had assumed was a good thing. He rose, met the ceiling with a sound like a dropped loaf, and stuck there face down, arms out, directly above the guards' card table.

There were two guards. They did not sound the alarm. They dealt him in. Sergeant Orla Brisk tilted her cards up so he could see them, and by the third hand Dabney was down 4 sp, which is the only kind of down he managed all night. The rest of the Seventh Spoon Company watched from the air vent and argued over whether rescuing him counted as part of the job or needed a separate contract.

Around the fifth hour a Driftsole courier owl came in through the vault's mail slot. I didn't know vaults got mail. Sergeant Brisk read the recall notice aloud to the ceiling: owners should not wear Featherstep slippers "indoors, near ceilings, or while committing crimes," and should take them off "over something soft." Driftsole is offering every owner a full refund or a complimentary cushion. A baker on Tanner's Row, also recalled, has been piping icing from his kitchen ceiling since Monday and reports that the cakes have never looked better.

The guards fetched a mattress. Dabney slipped off the slippers, dropped, and was arrested very gently. He asked me to print that the heist "was going well right up until it wasn't." In fairness, this is the town where another party once broadcast its heist plan to the whole village, so he did better than some.

Still! For the forty seconds the hover worked, it was the smoothest ride I have ever had, and that includes the carpet that parked over the market. Four out of five beholder eyes. I have already preordered version two. Byte tells me it ships with a ceiling subscription, which I hate, and which I will pay.

Damage Report: Rogues on ceilings: 1. Silver lost at cards, upside down: 4. Heists completed: 0. Eyebrows: fine, Dabney's less so.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

item.title: Rival Baronies RSVP to Feast; Seating Chart Is Now a Treaty
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: Ashenfold and Brackwater both said yes to the Grand Feast. The seating chart took nine hours of parley, and the wish spell turnips nearly sank it.
item.content:encoded:
Both baronies said yes. Ashenfold and Brackwater accepted their invitations to Brindlemoor's Grand Feast on Tuesday, and by Wednesday the seating chart had turned into a nine-hour parley. For newcomers: Feastwarden Odo Plumbrook has promised a feast for 2,000 on the Town Green on the 26th, on a budget of 900 gold pieces. Diplomacy was not in the budget. Neither, so far, is the goose.

He invited both baronies because nobody told him not to, and on Tuesday both of them wrote back.

The parley convened in the back room of the feast committee's rented hall. Envoy Halric Dunmere spoke for Ashenfold. Envoy Teodra Hallowmere spoke for Brackwater. Plumbrook stood on a chair between them holding a paper plan of the Green, which is where the trouble started. Handshake at the door: firm, two seconds, no hidden dagger detected. Hallowmere checked her own sleeve afterward anyway.

Ashenfold opened by demanding the table upwind of Brackwater. Brackwater asked for the same table. Both were told there is no wind on the Green in late autumn, and both refused to believe it. By the third hour the two delegations had agreed that neither would sit nearer the gravy than the other, and a committee clerk spent forty minutes measuring with string.

Then someone read the menu aloud. Item six: turnip mash, for 2,000.

Readers will recall the wish spell that turned 212 Ashenfold swords into turnips at an earlier parley. Brackwater still classes those turnips as weapons. Ashenfold calls them as its swords, temporarily vegetable. Plumbrook bought them at a discount last week because nobody else would, and he says he did not ask where they came from. "A turnip is a turnip," he told the room. Dunmere said this one was a longsword in the second rank. Hallowmere said serving it amounted to arming the guests.

Tension climbed to fourteen siege-days. It held there through two pots of tea.

The treaty signed at dusk runs to eleven clauses. Ashenfold sits on the east edge of the Green. Brackwater sits on the west. Between them runs a demilitarized strip four tables wide, held by the brass band. The salt is neutral. Clause nine creates a third table, the Turnip Table, where all 212 turnips will be served under guard. Neither barony will sit at it. Plumbrook has volunteered to sit there himself and called it "the best seat in the house." He has already asked whether there will be seconds.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor witnessed the signing. Asked whether a feast seating chart needed a reeve's seal, Reeve Fennick said, "It does now," and left.

Ottoline Vex has asked for a seat at the head table so she can describe the mood. She will get the Turnip Table. I filled in the request form myself.

Tension now holds at nine siege-days, down from fourteen. Clear objectives on both sides: eat, and be seen eating more. I respect it. I will be at the edge of the Green with field rations.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Cockatrice in Henhouse: Party Grabs 212 Chickens Bare-Handed
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: A cockatrice hid among 340 hens in Gorsewick. The party hired to catch it couldn't spot it, so they grabbed 212 chickens bare-handed. 17 are part stone.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, a cockatrice got into a hen farm in Gorsewick last week, and the adventuring party hired to clear it out could not tell which bird it was. So the Pluckwise Company picked up 212 chickens bare-handed, one at a time, and by Sunday evening our temple of healing in Brindlemoor had treated 17 cases of partial petrification.

The farm belongs to Bram Hollyweather, who keeps 340 hens and, as of Tuesday, one cockatrice he never ordered. "It came in under the fence and stood in the middle of the flock looking like a hen," he told me over his gate. "Well. From the back, anyway." He paid the Pluckwise 30 gold to take it away.

Their plan, as the party's fighter Tobin Marsh explained it to me from a cot in our east ward, was thorough. "Pick up each bird. Check it. Put it down." Nobody brought gloves. Nobody looked at the tails first, which is where the old herbals tell you to look, since a cockatrice drags a scaly one like a lizard's. Around the fortieth hen, the ranger's thumb went gray. By the ninetieth, the cleric had two stone fingers and was still volunteering. Tobin calls this resolve. I'd call it a party that never once asked a hen farmer.

Here's what happens, friends, for anyone tempted to try it. A cockatrice's peck stiffens the flesh where it lands, and if nobody treats it, the stiffness sets to stone within a day. We saw fingers, wrists, and a forearm that its owner now uses to hold doors. The party's bard went stone from his left ear down to the collarbone and sings only out of the right side of his mouth. He says his range has improved. It hasn't. Greater restoration fixes all of it, and the temple has cast it eleven times since Sunday, which is more than we cast it during the basilisk eye clinic business earlier this month.

The cockatrice was finally caught by Hollyweather's daughter, who is nine. She pointed through the fence and said, "That one's got a lizard bum." It was hen number 213. She caught it in a bucket.

The hens did not come through entirely clean either. Twenty-six eggs laid during the visit came out solid stone, and Hollyweather is selling them as doorstops at 2 silver apiece. He's sold out and keeps a waiting list. "They'll hold a door in a gale," he said, "and nobody's going to steal one for breakfast."

The old herbals claim a cockatrice hatches from a rooster's egg kept warm by a toad, which I doubt. The Brindlemoor Grangers' Fellowship's autumn count is more use: 14 cockatrice sightings near grain stores since harvest, because the pickings are easy. So look before you grab, and buy gloves; they cost 2 coppers. My friend Nyx tells me there's a scrying charm now that names any bird from a sketch. Go outside, Nyx. A nine-year-old did it from a fence.

For the stiff-fingered, I recommend a barley-and-mushroom soup, eaten slowly, with a spoon you can still bend your hand around. I'm leaving the chicken out this week, as a courtesy.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Nothic Sells Party's Heist Plan to Rivals for 5 Gold
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: An adventuring party rehearsed its vault job out loud eleven times. A nothic heard every word and sold it, rogue's real name and all, for 5 gold.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 4, 180 FEET DOWN — An adventuring party that spent three hours planning a vault job out loud in a Level Four corridor got to the vault Tuesday and found a rival party already there, holding a copy of the plan. The rivals say they bought it from a nothic for 5 gold pieces.

The planners, a five-member party called the Long Briefing, stopped in the east corridor outside the old counting vault to "go over it one more time." By their own count they went over it eleven times. They covered the marching order, the trap signal (two coughs), a fallback plan and a fallback for the fallback. At one point, to settle who got to say "go," somebody used the rogue's real name.

The rogue works as Whisper. His real name is Bertrand Fennimore Ottley. I know this because everyone on Level Four knows it now.

The nothic lives in a side passage about forty feet from where the party stood. It has one large eye and a steady trade in whatever drifts down that passage. "They never once checked the side passage," said Marn Esterby, captain of the rival Early Door Company, who was waiting at the vault with the marching order chalked on a slate. "We checked it. Five gold. It threw in the cough signal for free."

Esterby recited the plan back to the Long Briefing in full, both fallbacks included, then wished the rogue luck by his first name. Box score at the vault: fighter 31 hit points, cleric 22, wizard 14, rogue at full health and "emotionally at 3," per the party's bard, who asked to be named. The vault was empty anyway. The Early Door Company cleared it the night before.

The Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild, Chapter 9 says it has no rule against selling overheard plans and no plans to write one. A clerk confirmed the nothic holds no trading license, then pointed out that the license only covers trade above ground. Chapter 9's posted advice for Level Four, unchanged since spring, reads "Keep voices down." The Long Briefing say they read it aloud during the second run-through.

The party's wizard, Ilsabet Crane, stood by the method. "Planning is how you survive down here," she said. "We just did it near a nothic." Pressed, she admitted the party once held a planning session in a tavern booth next to a door marked "Nothic Consultations." I would call that a pattern. She called it bad luck.

For my part, I rolled poorly on where to stand. I stood in the side passage. The nothic sold my notes too, and I lost my thirteenth ten-foot pole of the season trying to fish them back out of its alcove. It now charges 2 silver to tell you where I keep the spares.

The Long Briefing say they will hit a different vault next week. They declined to say which one. Then they said which one, twice, while I was still in the corridor.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Frost Giant Clearing Snowed-In Pass Wants Giant-Sized Wages
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: A frost giant hired to clear Brindlemoor's snowed-in pass wants forty men's wages for forty men's work. The Reeve sent a spoon. A regular one.
item.content:encoded:
The frost giant wants wages sized like a giant.

Hrolgar Ninefathom, a frost giant hired Monday by Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor to clear the snowed-in Rimeback Pass, has asked for wages, rations, and a pension scaled to his size. The Reeve's office offered him the standard road-crew rate: 2 silver a day, one loaf, one bowl of stew, and a pension of a copper a year. He is twenty-one feet tall. He did the sums.

"My shovel is a barn door," Ninefathom told the Gazette, sitting down, which still put him level with the upstairs window of the toll house. "I move as much snow in a day as forty of your men. So pay me forty men. Feed me forty men. And pension me for as long as I live. That's a while."

By my count that comes to 8 gold a day, forty loaves, forty bowls of stew, and a pension the town would be paying for about three hundred more winters. The Reeve's treasury calls the request "a disproportionate compensation framework incompatible with standard scale." That means they said no.

Reeve Fennick's counteroffer came up a very tall ladder in a clerk's hand: one and a half wages, a double loaf, and what the scroll calls "an appropriately sized spoon." The spoon arrived Tuesday. I've seen it. It's a spoon.

So Ninefathom is working to rule. He clears what one and a half wages buys and not a shovelful more. By Wednesday morning the Rimeback Pass was open to a width of two feet, which suits a goat. Forty-one wagons of salt, lamp oil, and winter flour sit parked at the bottom. A goat went through at noon. The drivers booed it.

Down in the crew hut, the human shovelers back the giant. "He's asking to get paid for the work he does," said Gilda Ironpan, a road-crew shoveler of fourteen winters. "I've asked the same thing since I was a girl. If the big lad wins, I want my one wage paid on time. That'd be a first."

Osk Thimbleby, a baker on Fish Street, has already sent the Reeve a quote for forty loaves a day. "I'm not taking sides," he said. "I'm taking orders."

The Reeve's office warns that paying by size sets a bad precedent. Maybe. Pip Underbough, a halfling on the pass crew, has asked to have his wage cut to match his height, so long as his hours get cut to match too. The office hasn't answered him.

Big hirelings reading the fine print is a habit this month. An ettin porter asked for two shares, one per head, and got them. Ninefathom's ask is simpler. Forty men's work, forty men's wages. Any shop steward in Brindlemoor could do that sum on her fingers. I did it on mine.

Talks pick up Thursday at the toll house, once somebody fixes the clerk's ladder. The flour's still parked. The giant's still sitting in the snow, and he's in no hurry. He likes the cold.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Party Sent for 200 Geese Returns With 3 and a Griffon Egg
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: An adventuring party took 600 gp to market for 200 feast geese and came home with three geese and a griffon egg. I have counted the geese. There are three.
item.content:encoded:
Feastwarden Odo Plumbrook sent an adventuring party to the Brindlemoor market on Monday with 600 gp and a list with one word on it: geese, 200 of them, for the Grand Feast on the 26th. The party came back at dusk with three geese and a griffon egg. For anyone just joining us, the feast committee has 900 gp and has promised 2,000 guests dinner on the Town Green, so this was two thirds of the money. (I have counted the geese four times. There are still three.)

The party calls itself the Brass Spoon Company: four members, one cart. By their own account the shopping went well for about eleven minutes. They found Wennet Abbeyfield's pens on Tanner's Row, where 200 ordinary geese waited at 3 gp a bird, which comes to 600 gp exactly. Abbeyfield, who last week quoted the feast 600 gp for a single goose, says she had dropped the price out of pity. They bought three. "Then the bard said, 'Let's just look around first,'" she told me over her fence. "Thirty years I've sold geese. Nobody comes back after 'look around.'"

Around the corner, a stallholder in a very good hat had one egg on a velvet cushion. He told them it was a griffon egg, that grown griffons fetch a fortune, and that the price could only go up, and the market would sort out the rest. The party's wizard cast detect magic on it and reported "a faint glow, probably," which the rogue took as a yes. They paid 591 gp. The man in the hat folded up his cushion and has not been seen since.

Now the Loaf Index. At 4 copper a loaf, 591 gp is 14,775 loaves. The three geese cost 9 gp, or 225 loaves. A goose feeds about ten people, so the feast has thirty dinners covered and 1,970 to go, plus one egg, which feeds nobody until it hatches and then, I am told, wants feeding itself.

Wing-Marshal Corra Thistlebane of the Highcrest Griffon Riders' Lodge looked at the egg for me. Her verdict: probably real. "A griffon chick eats a horse a week by spring," she said. "Congratulations. You've bought a mouth." The Lodge offered 200 gp for it, a loss of 391 gp, or 9,775 loaves. (I did that sum in a stable, leaning on a horse. The horse did not enjoy the conversation either.)

Plumbrook, standing on a chair outside the Sleeping Mule, called the trip "a strong start." "Three geese is three more than we had this morning," he said. "And who else will have a griffon at their feast?" Nobody, I told him, since they can't afford one either. He turned down the Lodge's offer and has named the egg Gilbert, which I take as a poor sign for ever selling it.

My colleague Sterling Vanmoor calls Gilbert "an appreciating asset." So was the boar, Sterling, and Duchess is still eating two bushels of turnips a day. My aunt Marigold says her boot has never once come home with an egg in it.

What this means for your pantry: the committee has 300 gp left before the oven bill, nine days to go, and 1,970 dinners unbought. If you hold a feast ticket, eat beforehand.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Snowball Fight Turns to Ice Knife; Watch Takes 9 Wands
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A Fish Street snowball fight went sideways when an adventuring party's wizard cast Ice Knife. The City Watch took 9 wands off the street. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after noon, the first snow of the season came down on Brindlemoor, and by the fourth bell a friendly snowball fight on Fish Street had turned into Ice Knife. The City Watch allegedly confiscated nine wands before it was over. Nine. I counted them myself, from under a cart.

The trouble started with the Tin Whistle Company, a four-member adventuring party that rents rooms above the cooper's and had, by every account, a lovely morning. "It was snowballs. Normal snowballs," said Bryn Coldmarsh, the party's fighter, who was holding a bag of ice to her ear at the time. "Then Ottwin said he had a better snowball."

Ottwin Haverlee, the Company's wizard, allegedly cast Ice Knife at the party rogue, who was hiding behind a fishmonger's barrel. The shard missed the rogue. It did not miss the barrel, which went off like a frost bomb and covered half a block in sleet and herring. The rogue answered with a wand of magic missiles, "for fairness." The cleric then pulled a wand of web, allegedly to end the fighting, and glued six neighbors and one pigeon to a turnip cart. I have no sympathy for the pigeon.

Then the street joined in. The baker on the corner came out with a wand of fear. A retired sell-sword on the second floor produced a wand of wonder, and nobody can say what it did, except that it was purple and the snowman by the well now has opinions. "I came out to shovel my step," said Odile Fenn, who was holding a shovel at the time and still is, because it's frozen to her mitten.

Watch Sergeant Dorrick Plume arrived with eleven constables and a sack. "We collected nine wands, two scrolls, and one snowman we were told was a wizard in disguise," he said. "It was a snowman. It's still a snowman. Mostly." The wands sit in the Watch lockup until the thaw, or until somebody proves which one belongs to the baker.

The ninth wand, by the way, had a silver cap with a tiny garnet set in the end, and it caught the light off the snow in a way I can only describe as excellent. I held it for a minute. Anyway. I gave it back. Allegedly.

This is the second wizard in a month to get creative on Fish Street, after the fireball in the tavern back room, and the Watch has nailed a new notice to the well: snowballs only, made of snow, thrown by hand. Someone hit the notice with a snowball within the hour. My rival over at the dungeon desk would call the whole thing a tactical engagement. I call it a Monday with weather.

Haverlee says he'll pay for the barrel and most of the herring. "In my defense, it was a snowball," he told me. "It was just very fast and very pointy." The Tin Whistle Company is barred from snowball fights on Fish Street for the rest of the winter. The pigeon has not been charged.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Red Dragon and Lich Demand Feast Invites; Fire Marshal Says No
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: A red dragon says its rates paid for 311 of the Grand Feast's dinners. A lich wants a seat for his phylactery. The fire marshal wants neither one there.
item.content:encoded:
A young red dragon and a lich have each demanded a seat at the Grand Feast of Brindlemoor, and the town's fire marshal has asked that neither of them come. The feast, for those joining late, is the one the halfling Feastwarden Odo Plumbrook promised would feed 2,000 people on the Town Green on the 26th, on a budget of 900 gold pieces. Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor appointed him. She now refers to the appointment as "a decision I made."

The dragon's claim came first, by letter, on time. Skorvath keeps an 11,400-gold hoard under the old tannery on Tanner's Row and paid 140 gold pieces in hoard rates this year. The feast comes out of the town purse. By the dragon's arithmetic, set out over four pages with a summary, it has bought about 311 of the 2,000 dinners and would like to eat one of them. "I am a ratepayer," the gentleman from Tanner's Row wrote. "I ask what any ratepayer asks. A chair would be nice. I can also stand."

The lich's claim came second and ran longer. Councilor Maldrith Quennel, who sits for the Chandler Ward and has lived in a crypt on Chandler Lane for some three hundred years, argued that a sitting Burgess is invited to civic feasts by custom. He asked for one seat for himself and another for his phylactery, "which goes where I go, and is also, legally, me." He does not eat, he noted, so he would cost the committee nothing. He then requested sixty candles for ambience.

Fire Marshal Tamsin Coalhurst read both letters into the minutes at Sunday's committee meeting and objected to each. On the dragon: "The Green is permitted for cooking fires no larger than a cart. A young red dragon is a cooking fire that can walk." On the lich: "Sixty candles is sixty candles." She added that the committee already rents a salamander oven at 30 gold a day, and that the Green has, by her count, one bucket.

Feastwarden Plumbrook then stood on a chair and invited both. "Everyone is welcome at the Grand Feast," he said. "The dragon can sit by the oven. The oven will love it." My tally now puts the Feastwarden's Promises Made at fourteen and Promises Kept at none. The feast is ten days off, so in fairness none have come due.

Under the committee's rules, which I have read so you don't have to, seating belongs to the Subcommittee on Seating and fire belongs to the Marshal. Where the two overlap, "the Feastwarden shall decide, with regard to safety." The Feastwarden decided. The Marshal cited the town fire code, which outranks committee rules, and the question went up to the Reeve. "We are aware of the dragon," Reeve Fennick said. "We are also aware of the lich. I would like to be aware of fewer things."

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake said a compromise is forming: the dragon at the far end of the Green, downwind, beside the bucket, and the lich allowed twelve candles and the jar. Skorvath has written back accepting, and says it will bring its own bucket. Quennel has asked for the ruling in writing, along with forty-eight more candles, also in writing.

The Subcommittee on Seating meets Thursday to decide where everyone sits. It has not yet decided where to sit itself.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Magic Mouth Doorbell Recalled for Reciting Party's Password
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Gablecall's 25 gp Magic Mouth doorbell was meant to screen visitors. It read one party's password and heist plan to carol singers. Now it's recalled.
item.content:encoded:
Okay. OKAY. Gablecall Wardworks has recalled all 2,400 of its Porchmouth doorbells, a 25 gp Magic Mouth enchantment that bolts beside your door and screens visitors for you. The Snowlatch Company, a four-member adventuring party wintering in a rented mill house outside Brindlemoor, found the problem last Tuesday, when the doorbell greeted a troupe of carol singers by reciting the party's password.

The password is "Turnip Forty." I can print it now because roughly half of Brindlemoor already knows it.

I need you to understand how good this thing looked on paper. The Porchmouth runs on a firmware glyph Gablecall calls Smart Recall. Instead of one fixed message, the magic mouth listens to everything said within thirty feet of the door and "learns your household." The runic latency is zero. It speaks the moment a stranger steps on the mat. I preordered two!

Here is what the Snowlatch doorbell learned, according to the party's fighter, Agna Stoutbarrow. The password, obviously. The plan to rob the Thursday barrow on the Gorsewick road, including the bit where the rogue hides in the hay cart. And, worst of all, the bard's letter to his mother, which he had practiced aloud on the porch, and which apologized for the lute.

Then it told people. The carol singers got the password and the barrow plan, in verse, because the mouth matches the visitor's tone. The tax collector got the barrow plan and an itemized list of loot the party had described on the porch as "not technically income." A cultist handing out pamphlets got the bard's letter and left in tears.

"We bought it to guard our secrets," Stoutbarrow said, standing well away from her own door. "It is the only thing in this house that has never kept one."

Gablecall spokesman Fennet Oakhallow told me the Porchmouth "performed exactly as a very welcoming doorbell should" and that the recall is "a precaution against oversharing." Owners are asked to return units to the Gablecall shop on Fish Street. I went down there. The returned doorbells are stacked on a shelf, and every time a customer walks in, all of them recite their households' passwords at once. The shop now sounds like a choir that knows where you keep your coin.

The Snowlatch Company has changed its password and cancelled the barrow job. The tax collector has not cancelled anything. My familiar, Byte, a pseudodragon who now speaks only in ad copy, watched the whole thing and said, "Porchmouth: let your door do the talking." Byte has been asked to leave the mill house.

Still, the voice is gorgeous, and it never once mispronounced "Stoutbarrow." After last month's mimic door, a door that only talks feels like progress. Four out of five beholder eyes. Brother Tumbleberry will say I should simply knock and talk to my neighbors myself. Brother Tumbleberry has never heard a doorbell sing a heist plan in three-part harmony. I have. It was beautiful. I would like to hear it again.

Damage Report: Passwords leaked: 2 (theirs, and mine, since my preorder arrived this morning). Heists cancelled: 1. Bards consoled: 1. Eyebrows: fine.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

item.title: Winter Wolves Block Road; Both Baronies Hire Same Party
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: Ashenfold and Brackwater each hired one adventuring party to remove the winter wolves on the shared road. It was the same party, and the wolves have views.
item.content:encoded:
Seven winter wolves have blocked the road north of Quillmarch Bridge since the first snow fell on Firstday, and the baronies of Ashenfold and Brackwater each say the wolves belong to the other. Both hired an adventuring party to remove them. It was the same adventuring party.

Ashenfold moved first. Envoy Halric Dunmere signed the Copper Wick Company at noon for 300 gold to clear "Brackwater's wolves" off the road. At a quarter past two, Envoy Teodra Hallowmere signed the same five people for 300 gold to clear "Ashenfold's wolves." The company's fighter, a woman named Brisa Toll, accepted both purses. "Nobody asked if we were booked," she told this reporter. "That's on them."

I asked how she planned to tell the envoys. She said she planned not to.

The company reached the wolves at dusk. The plan was to kill wolves, collect 600 gold, and leave before either baron compared receipts. Then the largest wolf sat up in the snow and said, in clear Common, "Whose are we supposed to be?"

Her name is Rimetooth, and she speaks for the pack. She does not belong to Ashenfold, she says, and she does not belong to Brackwater, and she would like both baronies to stop putting it in writing. "We were on this road before either of your borders," she said. "We are the road's wolves. The road has not complained."

Then she asked the party what they were being paid. Brisa told her. Rimetooth asked who was paying. Brisa told her that too. The wolf laughed for some time.

The company's cleric tried to open terms. Rimetooth offered her paw. Firm, two seconds, no hidden dagger detected. Considerable claw. Her demands: the road stays shut each winter, both baronies route travelers over Quillmarch Bridge instead, and the troll there sends the pack one goat a week. Gorvash Pennyfist, the troll, has already refused. He blames goat prices.

Back in Ashenfold, Dunmere learned at breakfast that his hired swords also work for Brackwater. Hallowmere learned at the same breakfast, across the same table, because the two envoys still share a parley tent from the last round of border talks. Each now wants the other's 300 gold refunded to them. Neither wants the wolves. Both, according to the parley clerk who serves them breakfast, would accept the wolves if the paperwork named them as the other side's.

The Copper Wick Company has done nothing for two days. Brisa calls this "holding the line." She is eating field rations by a fire in sight of the pack, which I respect. The rations are terrible. I had two.

So the count stands at seven winter wolves, five adventurers, two contracts, and zero baronies willing to own a wolf. Tension sits at fourteen siege-days. The wolves, for the record, are sleeping fine.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Tiered Seating Bid for Feast of 2,000: Chairs Are Gold Tier
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: I bid on the Grand Feast catering: a Heroes' Feast spell for 12 Platinum guests, chairs at Gold, and a free tier near the boar. I call it disruption.
item.content:encoded:
On Saturday I submitted a formal bid to cater the Grand Feast of Brindlemoor, the free feast for 2,000 that Feastwarden Odo Plumbrook has promised on the Town Green on the 26th with a 900 gp budget. My plan is called Feast as a Service. It sorts guests into four tiers, and the top one gets a Heroes' Feast spell cast by a hired cleric. It's catering that scales, friends.

Some background for the three people in town who haven't heard. Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor named the halfling Feastwarden, and he promised two thousand plates before anyone had written a menu. The menu now costs 4,300 gp. That 3,400 gp gap is what I call unmet demand.

So here are the tiers. Platinum is 40 gp a seat, capped at 12, because the spell feeds 12 and I respect a hard limit. Gold is 5 gp and includes a chair. Silver is 1 gp: a bench, a plate, and a potato, peeled by volunteers who are, I'm told, extremely well exposed. Bronze is free. Bronze guests stand at the east end of the Green, directly downwind of the roast, and may smell anything they like.

Is the smell of a boar worth a silver? My numbers say a Bronze guest smells it for about four hours, and every guest who drifts down to Bronze is a plate the town never buys. I call that rightsizing the adventuring party, where the party happens to be the whole town.

The town's cost is a single 900 gp onboarding fee. Yes, that's the whole budget. I see it as alignment.

Plumbrook read the proposal standing on a chair at the committee table. "It's a strong start," he said, and then someone from my team gently told him the chair was Gold tier. He stayed up there anyway, which is exactly the energy I want in a client.

The Reeve was less visionary. "We are aware of the bid," Reeve Fennick said, and asked whether Bronze guests would be fed at all. They would be fed by aroma, Your Worship. Aroma is food in a lighter format.

About the roast. The centerpiece is Duchess, the giant boar who currently rents the big stall at the Sleeping Mule and has not agreed to be dinner. Keeper Bess Harrowgate says house rule six still applies. Fine. In my revised deck, Platinum guests get a meet-and-greet with Duchess instead. Experiences come in tiers. I borrowed that from Cinderlatch Works, whose oven pricing I admire the way some men admire sunsets.

I once shared a balloon basket with Guildmaster Tobrin Ashgrove over the Thornwood. He looked down at all those boars and said, "Sterling, everybody eats. Not everybody eats first." I wrote it on my sword-practice dummy, and I read it every morning at five.

I expect a certain columnist who peels potatoes for solidarity to call this a velvet rope around dinner. Brakka, a rope is just a line with a business model.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

• Scarcity is a menu item.
• Never sell a chair you can rent.
• If the boar won't sign, upsell the boar.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Hold Person Freezes Heckler Mid-Sneer; Spell Ban Takes 3 Hours
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: A wizard froze a heckling Burgess with Hold Person at her party's damage hearing. Brindlemoor then banned spellcasting, after three hours of debate.
item.content:encoded:
A wizard testifying before Brindlemoor's Burgess Council on Friday cast Hold Person on a Burgess who was heckling her, freezing him mid-sneer for one full minute. The Council answered by voting to ban spellcasting during debate. Debate on the ban took three hours.

The wizard, Mirela Tansy of the Overdue Ledger Company, had been called to answer for a 2,300 gold damage bill. The charge sheet lists a chandlery roof, most of a hedge maze, and a public fountain that now contains frogs nobody has been able to account for. It was the second adventuring party in a week to bring its spells to a hearing in this Chamber, after the party whose Zone of Truth confession cost three Burgesses their seats. The Council is starting to take it personally.

The heckler was the gentleman from Tanners' Row, Burgess Osric Dunmallow, who interrupted Tansy fourteen times in her first six minutes. The minutes, which I keep more accurately than the Clerk does, record his interjections as "frogs, really," "tell it to the hedge," "frogs," and a long, curling sneer, which is where the spell found him. For sixty seconds the gentleman from Tanners' Row sat with his mouth open to the rafters and one finger raised, as though about to make a point of order. A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake called it "the most productive minute of his term."

Tansy told the Chamber she had cast the spell "in the spirit of decorum." Presiding Burgess Hettie Gorse ruled that decorum does not include paralysis. Tansy asked whether it could, and was ruled out of order. Dunmallow, once released, finished the sneer.

The motion to ban spellcasting during debate was introduced at a quarter past two. It was one sentence long. The lady from Millgate moved to amend it to exempt Light, so the Chamber could see after dark. The gentleman from the Lower Quays moved to exempt Prestidigitation, for warming tea. A third Burgess asked whether a cantrip counted as a spell or as a habit, and spoke to the question for forty minutes. At one point a Burgess proposed that someone cast Silence on the debate to end it. The Clerk observed that this would itself be spellcasting during debate, and the proposal was referred to committee.

The ban passed 6-3 at a quarter past five. It applies to witnesses and the gallery. It does not apply to Burgesses, a carve-out the lady from Millgate called "only sensible." By my tally, this session's Promises Made stand at nine and Promises Kept at none. The promise to finish by three is one of the nine.

The damage bill itself was never reached. It has been carried over to next month, along with the frogs. The Overdue Ledger Company says it will appeal, and that its wizard has promised to come with no spells prepared, which Gorse called "the least reassuring thing I have heard all day."

The motion carried. Nobody read the amendments.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Roper Was the Stalagmite the Ranger Leaned On
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: The Fourth Attempt's ranger leaned on a stalagmite to catch his breath on Level 6. It was warm. It had an eye. It was a roper. Hit points tallied.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 6, A HUNDRED AND TEN FEET DOWN — The Fourth Attempt's ranger stopped to catch his breath in a Level 6 cavern on Thursday and leaned his whole weight on the nearest stalagmite. It was a roper. By its own account, which it gave with one eye, it had been standing there since harvest.

The party had just come up a long scree slope, and the ranger was at the back of it, which is where he has been walking since the business with the upside-down map. He put a hand on the rock. Then a shoulder. "It was warm," he told me afterward, still a little out of breath. "I thought there was a hot spring under it. I thought, finally, something down here is being nice to me."

The roper opened its eye at about the height of his elbow. Its tendrils took him around the middle and lifted him four feet off the cavern floor, and he stayed up there for the better part of a minute while the rest of the Fourth Attempt worked out what to hit.

That took a while. "There were eleven stalagmites in that cave," said the party's bard, who asked to be named. "You can't just swing at geology." The fighter swung at geology anyway, twice, and chipped a perfectly innocent stalagmite before finding the guilty one. The wizard would not cast anything with fire in it until somebody counted the rocks. The cleric settled it with a mace to the eye, and the roper let go and went up the wall, slowly and with what I can only call dignity, into a crack in the ceiling. It is presumed to be up there still, pretending.

Box score at the top of the slope: ranger 6 hit points (of 29), fighter 30 (of 38), cleric 24 (of 30), wizard 22 (of 22), bard untouched and already writing a verse about it. One stalagmite chipped. No charges filed by the stalagmite.

Ansel Pottage, steward of the party's hirelings, read the relevant clause aloud at camp. The hirelings' contract carries a hazard rider for mimics that covers "furniture, doors, and chests." It says nothing about scenery. "Rocks were never in the clause," Pottage said, rewrapping a bandage. "We've been leaning on rocks for years." He has filed with Chapter 9 to add "any formation taller than a dwarf" to the hazard schedule. A Chapter 9 clerk told me the guild map marks Level 6 as mostly cleared and the cavern as "decorative."

For the record, I lost my twelfth ten-foot pole of the season in there. I tap every stalagmite on the way into a cave, as any torchbearer should, but I rolled poorly on the order and started from the far end. The roper took the pole with it on the way up the wall. I am told they do that.

The ranger has been seen resting since. He sits on the floor now. He checks the floor first.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Identify Fees Jump 60%, So Party Tests Its Loot by Drinking It
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: Identify fees in Brindlemoor rose 60% to 240 gp, so a party holding 40 unidentified magic items began drinking and wearing them. I did the sums.
item.content:encoded:
Identify fees in Brindlemoor have risen 60% this month, from 150 gp an item to 240 gp, as the autumn loot glut backs up every sage's counter on Sages' Lane. On Monday the Pickled Griffons, a four-member adventuring party, carried 40 unidentified magic items up out of the Undermaw and learned that identifying all of them would cost 9,600 gp, about four times the only offer anyone had made for the lot.

On the Loaf Index, 9,600 gp is 205,344 loaves. (I have checked this four times. I lay down after the second.) The offer came from Odalys Marrow of Marrow & Finch Curios, who bid 2,400 gp for the whole sack, unopened. "I don't know what's in it either," Marrow said. "That's what the 2,400 is for."

Why 60%? I made a spreadsheet, and I'm afraid it's simple. The identify spell eats a pearl worth at least 100 gp every time it is cast. Brindlemoor has six sages who can cast it, and each manages about eleven a day. Every party in town wants its haul sorted before the snow. Demand has roughly doubled while the supply of sages has stayed at six. "My waiting list runs to midwinter," said Master Edric Pellow, who has started charging 5 gp just to be put on it.

So the Griffons went the cheap way. "You put it on," explained their wizard, Corran Bisk, who knows the spell but not where to get the pearls cheap. "If something happens, now you know what it does."

Several things happened, mostly to the fighter. Dunstan Roe drank a potion of climbing and spent Tuesday on the ceiling of the Ladle & Lamp common room, declining to come down because the floor "looked uncertain." The rogue drank a potion of diminution and is now six inches tall and in talks with the inn cat. A ring of swimming was identified in a horse trough. Bisk drank a potion of healing while perfectly healthy ("I feel the same, only more expensive"). Brother Aldous Venn put on a helm of comprehending languages and now understands the inn parrot, which he says is worse than not understanding it. One flask was a potion of poison. And a small oak chest turned out to be a mimic when Roe sat on it.

By Wednesday the party had identified 31 of the 40, at a temple bill of 410 gp. At sage rates those 31 would have cost 7,440 gp. My colleague Sterling Vanmoor calls this "price discovery" and says the market will sort itself out. The market has put a fighter on the ceiling, Sterling.

The Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild, Chapter 9, reminds members that an hour of quiet attention with an item will often reveal what it does, free of charge. The Griffons said they did not have an hour, and then spent three days on it. The last nine items include a pair of boots nobody will touch. My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, says you never put your foot in a boot you found in a hole. I used to laugh at her. I have stopped.

What this means for your pantry: one identify is now 5,134 loaves, and an unidentified potion is still not a beverage.
